title.en: The Saucy Indians Who Became Rattlesnakes
title.zh: 無禮的印第安人化為響尾蛇

region.en: Passamaquoddy country before the Great Flood
region.zh: 大洪水之前的帕薩馬科迪之地

texts.period: Passamaquoddy tale related by an old woman to Mrs. W. Wallace Brown (Leland 1884)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'How Glooskap changed Certain Saucy Indians into Rattlesnakes'

summary.en: Long time ago the Rattlesnakes were saucy Indians - they had too much face, and could not be put down by much, and they got up for very little. When the great Flood was coming Glooskap told them about it; they said they did not care. 'The Flood will come and drown you all' - then these Indians hurrahed again, got their rattles made of turtle-shells fastened together and filled with pebbles, and had a grand dance. The rain began to fall, but they danced; the thunder roared, and they shook their rattles and yelled at it. Then Glooskap was angry: he did not drown them in the Flood, but changed them into rattlesnakes. Nowadays, when they see a man coming, they lift up their heads and move them about - that's the way snakes dance - and they shake the rattles in their tails just as Indians shake their rattles when they dance.
summary.zh: 很久以前，響尾蛇原是一群無禮的印第安人——架子極大，軟硬不吃，動輒起鬨。大洪水將至，格魯斯卡普勸告他們，他們卻說毫不在乎。「洪水將至，要淹死你們全體！」——這些印第安人再次歡呼，取來龜殼串成、內填碎石的老式響鈴，跳起大舞。大雨落下，他們照舞；雷霆轟鳴，他們搖鈴吼叫以對。格魯斯卡普怒了——他不在洪水中淹死他們，而是把他們化為響尾蛇。如今蛇見人來，便昂首擺動——那是蛇的舞蹈——尾鈴搖動，正如印第安人跳舞時搖鈴一般。

sensitivity.note: Passamaquoddy tale (Leland 1884); public domain. A flood-and-transgression aition in the NE Woodlands register.

passages.text: You know At-o-sis, the Snake? Well, the worst of all is Rattlesnake. Long time ago the Rattlesnakes were saucy Indians. They were very saucy. They had too much face. They could not be put down by much, and they got up for very little. When the great Flood was coming Glooskap told them about it. They said they did not care. He told them the water would come over their heads. They said that would be very wet. He told them to be good and quiet, and pray. Then those Indians hurrahed. He said, 'A great Flood is coming.' Then they gave three cheers for the great Flood. He said, 'The Flood will come and drown you all.' Then these Indians hurrahed again, and got their rattles, made of turtle-shells, in the old fashion, fastened together, filled with pebbles, and rattled them and had a grand dance.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 110-111; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Yes, they had a great dance. The rain began to fall, but they danced. The thunder roared, and they shook their rattles and yelled at it. Then Glooskap was angry. He did not drown them in the Flood, however, but he changed them into rattlesnakes. Nowadays, when they see a man coming, they lift up their heads and move them about. That's the way snakes dance. And they shake the rattles in their tails just as Indians shake their rattles when they dance. How do you like such music?
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, p. 111; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: Glooskap Binds Wuchowsen, the Great Wind-Bird
title.zh: 格魯斯卡普縛住風鳥伍喬森

region.en: Great rock at the end of the sky, far to the North

texts.period: Passamaquoddy manuscript collection by Louis Mitchell (Leland 1884)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'How Glooskap bound Wuchowsen, the Great Wind-Bird'

summary.en: The Indians believe in a great bird called Wochowsen or Wuchowsen, meaning Wind-Blow, who lives far to the North and sits upon a great rock at the end of the sky; whenever he moves his wings the wind blows. When it blew a tempest so that Glooskap could not go out at all, he sought the Bird-giant: 'You take no compassion on your Koosesek, your grandchildren. You have caused this wind and storm; it is too much. Be easier with your wings!' 'I have been here since ancient times... mine was the first voice, and I will ever move my wings as I will.' Then Glooskap rose in his might to the clouds, took the Great Bird-giant as though he were a duck, tied both his wings, and threw him down into a chasm between deep rocks. The Indians could now go out in their canoes all day long - but with that all the waters became stagnant, so thick that Glooskap could not paddle. Then he raised Wuchowsen, who is immortal, put him on his rock again, and untied one of his wings; since then the winds have never been so terrible as in the old time.
summary.zh: 印第安人信奉大鳥伍喬森——「吹風者」——居極北，坐在天際盡頭的巨岩上；牠一振翅，風便吹起。暴風大到格魯斯卡普無法出舟時，他前去尋這鳥中巨人：「你竟不憐惜你的孫兒們。這風暴皆你所致，太過分了！收斂些翅膀吧！」「自太古我便在此……最初的聲音便出於我翅，我永遠要隨心振翅。」格魯斯卡普躍上雲端，如提鴨般拎起巨鳥，縛其雙翅，擲入深岩之隙。此後印第安人終日泛舟——然而天下之水皆成死水，濃稠得連舟都划不動。主人便再扶起不朽的伍喬森，放回岩上，解其一翼——自那以後，風再沒有上古時那樣狂暴。

sensitivity.note: Passamaquoddy tale (Leland 1884); public domain. Leland compares Wuchowsen to the Norse Hraesvelg and stresses he is a wind-bird, not the western thunder-bird.

passages.text: The Indians believe in a great bird called by them Wochowsen or Wuchowsen, meaning Wind-Blow or the Wind-Blower, who lives far to the North, and sits upon a great rock at the end of the sky. And it is because whenever he moves his wings the wind blows they of old times called him that. When Glooskap was among men he often went out in his canoe with bow and arrows to kill sea-fowl. At one time it was every day very windy; it grew worse; at last it blew a tempest, and he could not go out at all. Then he said, 'Wuchowsen, the Great Bird, has done this!' He went to find him; it was long ere he reached his abode. He found sitting on a high rock a large white Bird.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 111-112; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: 'Grandfather,' said Glooskap, 'you take no compassion on your Koosesek, your grandchildren. You have caused this wind and storm; it is too much. Be easier with your wings!' The Giant Bird replied, 'I have been here since ancient times; in the earliest days, ere aught else spoke, I first moved my wings; mine was the first voice - and I will ever move my wings as I will.' Then Glooskap rose in his might; he rose to the clouds; he took the Great Bird-giant Wuchowsen as though he were a duck, and tied both his wings, and threw him down into a chasm between deep rocks, and left him lying there.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 112-113; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: The Indians could now go out in their canoes all day long, for there was a dead calm for many weeks and months. And with that all the waters became stagnant. They were so thick that Glooskap could not paddle his canoe. Then he thought of the Great Bird, and went to see him. As he had left him he found him, for Wuchowsen is immortal. So, raising him, he put him on his rock again, and untied one of his wings. Since then the winds have never been so terrible as in the old time.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, p. 113; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: The Great Bull-Frog: The River Made Flesh and the First Water Creatures
title.zh: 巨牛蛙：化為血肉的大河與最初的水族

region.en: Mountain village on a brook, and the up-country dam
region.zh: 溪畔的山村與上游的水壩

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'How Glooskap conquered the Great Bull-Frog'

summary.en: A village by a brook - the only water in all the country round - watches the stream dry to a dead bone. Upstream a monster chief, immense, bloated, with yellow eyes stuck out like pine-knots and a mouth from ear to ear, has dammed the rivulet for nothing, and bellows 'Do as you choose... If you want water, go somewhere else.' Glooskap comes among the honest villagers dressed terribly ferocious - ten feet high, a hundred feathers, clam-shells at each ear - bade them be of good cheer, and at the monster's town demands water: thrusting a spear into his belly, there gushed forth a mighty river, even all the water which should have run on while in the rivulet, for he had made it into himself. Glooskap crumpled his back with a mighty grip - it was the Bull-Frog, whose back bears the prints to this day - and hurled him into the stream. Meanwhile, in the hour when all wishes are granted, the simple villagers had wished themselves into the soft mud, the diving rocks, the rippling waves and the water forever: the first became a Leech, the second a Spotted Frog, the third a Crab, and the fourth a Fish - for ere this there had been in all the world none of the creatures which dwell in the water.
summary.zh: 山村傍溪而居——四野僅此一水——卻眼看溪水枯竭如死骨。上游的怪酋巨大臃腫、黃眼如松節、口裂至耳，平白築壩攔水，咆哮著「隨你們便……要水，另找去」。格魯斯卡普氣勢駭人地來到村中——身高十呎、頂插百羽、耳掛蛤殼——安慰村民，直搗怪酋之城索水；一矛刺入其腹，滔滔大河傾瀉而出——原來整條溪水都被他吞化於己身。主人如握巨松般捏彎其背——正是牛蛙，其背至今留著那可怕的指痕——隨手擲入溪流。同時，在「萬願得償」的那個時辰，純樸的村民許願入軟泥、躍岩潛水、隨波起伏、永居水中：第一人化為水蛭，第二人化為斑蛙，第三人化為螃蟹，第四人化為魚——在此之前，世上從無棲水之物。

sensitivity.note: Passamaquoddy tale (Leland 1884); public domain. Leland notes the bull-frog is the river incarnate - the ice of winter pierced by the spear of the sun.

passages.text: Of old times, there was an Indian village far away among the mountains, little known to other men... The town was by a brook, and except in it there was not a drop of water in all the country round, unless in a few rain-puddles. No one there had ever found even a spring. But after a time they began to observe that the brook was beginning to run low, and that not in the summer time, but in autumn, even after the rains. And day by day it diminished, until its bed was as dry as a dead bone in the ashes of a warm fire. Now it was said that far away up in the land where none had ever been there was on this very stream another Indian village; but what manner of men dwelt therein no one knew.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 114-115; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: And after he had traveled three days he came to the place; and there he found that a dam had been raised across the rivulet, so that no water could pass, for it was all kept in a pond. Then asking them why they had made this mischief, since the dam was of no use to them, they bade him go and see their chief, by whose order this had been built. And when he came to him, lo, there lay lazily in the mud a creature who was more of a monster than a man, though he had a human form. For he was immense to measure, like a giant, fat, bloated, and brutal to behold. His great yellow eyes stuck from his head like pine-knots, his mouth went almost from ear to ear, and he had broad, skinny feet with long toes, exceeding marvelous. The messenger complained to this monster, who at first said nothing, and then croaked, and finally replied in a loud bellow: 'Do as you choose... If you want water, go somewhere else.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 115-116; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Then Glooskap, who was much pleased with all this, for he loved a brave man, came among them looking terribly ferocious; in all the land there was not one who seemed half so horrible. For he appeared ten feet high, with a hundred red and black feathers in his scalp-lock, his face painted like fresh blood with green rings round his eyes, a large clam-shell hanging from each ear, a spread eagle, very awful to behold, flapping its wings from the back of his neck... 'Give me to drink, and that of the best, at once, thou Thing of Mud!' But the chief reviled him, and said, 'Get thee hence, to find water where thou canst.' Then Glooskap thrust a spear into his belly, and lo! there gushed forth a mighty river; even all the water which should have run on while in the rivulet, for he had made it into himself. And Glooskap, rising high as a giant pine, caught the chief in his hand and crumpled in his back with a mighty grip. And lo! it was the Bull-Frog. So he hurled him with contempt into the stream, to follow the current. And ever since that time the Bull-Frog's back has crumpled wrinkles in the lower part, showing the prints of Glooskap's awful squeeze.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 117-118; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Then he returned to the village; but there he found no people - no, not one. For a marvelous thing had come to pass during his absence, which shall be heard in every Indian's speech through all the ages. For the men, being, as I said, simple, honest folk, did as boys do when they are hungry, and say unto one another, 'What would you like to have, and what you?' Even so these villagers had said, 'Suppose you had all the nice cold, fresh, sparkling, delicious water there is in the world, what would you do?' And one said that he would live in the soft mud, and always be wet and cool. And another, that he would plunge from the rocks, and take headers, diving into the deep, cold water, drinking as he dived. And the third, that he would be washed up and down with the rippling waves, living on the land, yet ever in the water. Then the fourth said, 'Verily, you know not how to wish, and I will teach you. I would live in the water all the time, and swim about in it forever.' Now it chanced that these things were said in the hour which, when it passes over the world, all the wishes uttered by men are granted. And so it was with these Indians. For the first became a Leech, the second a Spotted Frog, the third a Crab, which is washed up and down with the tide, and the fourth a Fish. Ere this there had been in all the world none of the creatures which dwell in the water, and now they were there, and of all kinds. And the river came rushing and roaring on, and they all went headlong down to the sea, to be washed into many lands over all the world.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 118-119; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: Glooskap and the Mighty Wasis: The Invincible Baby
title.zh: 格魯斯卡普與偉大的瓦西斯：不敗的嬰兒

region.en: The sunny lodge floor where Wasis sits
region.zh: 瓦西斯安坐的向陽屋地

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'How the Lord of Men and Beasts strove with the Mighty Wasis'

summary.en: When Glooskap had conquered all his enemies - the giants and sorcerers, the magicians, Pamola the evil spirit of the night air, all manner of ghosts, witches, devils, cannibals and goblins - he wondered if his work was at an end. 'Not so fast, Master, for there yet remains One whom no one has ever conquered... It is the mighty Wasis, and there he sits; and I warn you that if you meddle with him you will be in sore trouble.' Now Wasis was the Baby, and he sat on the floor sucking a piece of maple-sugar. The Master smiled sweetly, spoke terribly, and at last had recourse to magic - used his most awful spells, and sang the songs which raise the dead and scare the devils. And Wasis sat and looked on admiringly, and seemed to find it very interesting, but all the same he never moved an inch. So Glooskap gave it up in despair, and Wasis went goo! goo! and crowed. And to this day when you see a babe well contented, going goo! goo! and crowing, and no one can tell why, know that it is because he remembers the time when he overcame the Master who had conquered all the world. For of all the beings that have ever been since the beginning, Baby is alone the only invincible one.
summary.zh: 當格魯斯卡普降服了所有敵手——巨人與巫者、術士、夜氣惡靈帕莫拉，以及一切鬼魅巫妖——他自問功成之業是否已畢。「莫急，主人。尚有一位從未被任何人降服者……那便是偉大的瓦西斯；他就坐在那裡。我警告你，若去招惹他，你必大吃苦頭。」瓦西斯就是嬰兒，正坐在地上含著一塊楓糖。主人先是甜笑柔聲，繼而疾言厲色，最後動用法術——唸起最可畏的咒語，唱起能喚死者、懾鬼魅之歌。瓦西斯只是饒有興味地看著，寸步不動。格魯斯卡普只得絕望作罷；瓦西斯坐在陽光裡「咯咯」而笑。至今嬰兒無故咯咯而笑時，那是他記起了戰勝「征服全世界之主」的那一刻——自開天闢地以來，唯有嬰兒是無敵的。

sensitivity.note: Penobscot tale (Leland 1884); public domain. Leland calls its Indian author 'a genius' and dates the tale ancient because it explains the unaccountable crowing of babies.

passages.text: Now it came to pass when Glooskap had conquered all his enemies, even the Kewahqu, who were giants and sorcerers, and the m'teoulin, who were magicians, and the Pamola, who is the evil spirit of the night air, and all manner of ghosts, witches, devils, cannibals, and goblins, that he thought upon what he had done, and wondered if his work was at an end. And he said this to a certain woman. But she replied, 'Not so fast, Master, for there yet remains One whom no one has ever conquered or got the better of in any way, and who will remain unconquered to the end of time.' 'And who is he?' inquired the Master. 'It is the mighty Wasis,' she replied, 'and there he sits; and I warn you that if you meddle with him you will be in sore trouble.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 120-121; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Now Wasis was the Baby. And he sat on the floor sucking a piece of maple-sugar, greatly contented, troubling no one. As the Lord of Men and Beasts had never married or had a child, he knew naught of the way of managing children. Therefore he was quite certain, as is the wont of such people, that he knew all about it. So he turned to Baby with a bewitching smile and bade him come to him. Then Baby smiled again, but did not budge. And the Master spake sweetly and made his voice like that of the summer bird, but it was of no avail, for Wasis sat still and sucked his maple-sugar. Then the Master frowned and spoke terribly, and ordered Wasis to come crawling to him immediately. And Baby burst out into crying and yelling, but did not move for all that.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, p. 121; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Then, since he could do but one thing more, the Master had recourse to magic. He used his most awful spells, and sang the songs which raise the dead and scare the devils. And Wasis sat and looked on admiringly, and seemed to find it very interesting, but all the same he never moved an inch. So Glooskap gave it up in despair, and Wasis, sitting on the floor in the sunshine, went goo! goo! and crowed. And to this day when you see a babe well contented, going goo! goo! and crowing, and no one can tell why, know that it is because he remembers the time when he overcame the Master who had conquered all the world. For of all the beings that have ever been since the beginning, Baby is alone the only invincible one.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 121-122; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
